ch03.note: A play on Lu Xiaofeng’s name. The princess is Danfeng (丹凤), ‘scarlet phoenix’; Lu’s given name Xiaofeng (小凤) is ‘little phoenix.’ The child is correcting him: it is Princess Scarlet-Phoenix who has come, not some Princess named after him. Her surname, and the whole royal house’s, proves to be Shangguan — the same borne by Shangguan Feiyan of the Prologue.

A pun that does not survive into English. Chinese jiugui (酒鬼), literally ‘wine-ghost,’ is the everyday word for a drunkard. Told there is a ‘ghost’ (gui) in the jar that will not break, Dugu Fang answers that it is of course a wine-ghost — a sot — the only kind of ghost a wine-jar would keep.

Lu You (陆游, 1125–1210), styled Fangweng (放翁, ‘the old man set free’), was among the best-loved poets of the Southern Song and a fervent patriot, of whose verses thousands survive. He shares the surname Lu with Lu Xiaofeng, but no kinship is implied: the whole speech is Lu Xiaofeng inventing a priceless pedigree for a plain hut in order to fleece the child, and the ‘master craftsman Lu Zhi’ a few lines earlier is very likely invented too.

ch03.anchor: Lust is a blade that scrapes the bone
ch03.note: A well-worn folk couplet — se shi guagu gangdao, jiu shi chuanchang duyao (色是刮骨钢刀，酒是穿肠毒药), ‘lust is a steel knife that scrapes the bone, wine a poison that pierces the gut’ — from the moralising tradition that warns against the four vices of wine, lust, wealth and wrath. Xiao Qiuyu quotes it drily as his warrant for smashing the jars.

ch04.anchor: Then why did you come to the Central Lands
ch04.note: Zhongtu (中土), ‘the central land,’ is China proper, the settled agrarian heartland, named here from the vantage of a frontier people for whom it is the centre of the civilised world. The kingdom of the Golden Roc lies somewhere out beyond its western marches.

The Cossacks — horse-borne warrior communities of the Eurasian steppe, north of the Black and Caspian Seas — are an anachronism here, of a piece with Gu Long’s deliberately vague, half-legendary geography. Their mention places the fallen kingdom of the Golden Roc far out on the north-western frontier, beyond the passes, among the powers of the steppe.

Mount Emei (峨嵋) in Sichuan is one of the sacred mountains of Chinese Buddhism; in martial-arts fiction it is also the seat of a great sword-school, a pillar of the jianghu beside Shaolin and Wudang. That its upright and public master should secretly be the traitor Dugu Yihe is the very scandal the Great King’s demand would lay bare.

A spirit-tablet (灵位, lingwei) is an inscribed wooden tablet that houses the soul of the dead for veneration; it stands on the ancestral altar and receives offerings and the reporting of family affairs. To repent one’s crime before the old King’s tablet is to make confession directly to his spirit.

Shaolin (少林), the Chan Buddhist monastery on Mount Song in Henan, and Wudang (武当), the Taoist mountain in Hubei, are the two most storied martial traditions of Chinese fiction — the Buddhist ‘hard, outer’ and Taoist ‘soft, inner’ schools. Lu Xiaofeng is naming the handful of men he reckons to have reached the summit of the martial arts; that Huo Xiu and Dugu Yihe stand among them is the measure of how formidable the Great King’s two chief enemies are.

An allusion to the classic novel Water Margin, in which the innkeepers Sun Erniang and Zhang Qing drug lone travellers with knock-out wine and grind the bodies into the stuffing of steamed buns (renrou baozi, 人肉包子). Lu Xiaofeng’s closing joke — that he hopes the night’s fare is not man-flesh buns, nor the drink a soul-stealing wine — casts the eerie, half-empty mansion of the Golden Roc as just such a bandit inn.
